notes:
Force on Moving Charge & Current

  • Lorentz force: $\vec{F} = q(\vec{E}+\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$; magnetic force alone $F = qvB\sin\theta$, direction by right-hand rule, does no work (always $\perp v$).
  • Force on a current-carrying conductor: $F = BIl\sin\theta$; force per unit length between two long parallel wires carrying $I_1$, $I_2$ at separation $d$: $\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ — like currents attract, unlike repel. This defines the SI ampere.

Biot–Savart Law & Field due to Currents

SourceField
Infinite straight wire$B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}$
Centre of circular loop ($N$ turns, radius $R$)$B=\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{2R}$
On axis of circular loop, distance $x$$B=\dfrac{\mu_0NIR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}$
Ideal solenoid (n = turns/length)$B=\mu_0nI$
Toroid$B=\mu_0nI$ (n = turns per unit circumference)
  • Ampere's circuital law: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0I_{enc}$.

Circular Motion & Cyclotron

  • Charge in a magnetic field alone moves in a circle: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, period $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ (independent of speed) — basis of the cyclotron. Cyclotron frequency $f=\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}$.
  • Velocity selector: undeflected when $qE = qvB \Rightarrow v = E/B$.

Torque on a Current Loop & Moving Coil Galvanometer

  • Magnetic moment of a loop: $m = NIA$; torque in field $\vec{\tau} = \vec{m}\times\vec{B}$, magnitude $\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$.
  • Galvanometer: current sensitivity $= NAB/k$ ($k$= torsional constant); converted to ammeter by a low shunt resistance in parallel, to voltmeter by a high resistance in series.
  • Shunt for ammeter of range $n$ times $I_g$: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{(n-1)I_g} = \dfrac{G}{n-1}$. Series resistance for voltmeter: $R = \dfrac{V}{I_g}-G$.

Exam tip

One of the highest-weightage chapters (3–4 KCET questions): expect a force-between-wires or force-on-conductor numerical, a Biot–Savart/solenoid field calculation, and a galvanometer-to-ammeter/voltmeter conversion problem. Get comfortable with the right-hand rule for direction-based questions.

questions.q: A charged particle moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$. The magnetic force on it is used to provide centripetal force. The radius of its circular path is
questions.explanation: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
questions.trick: $qvB=mv^2/r$ gives $r=mv/qB$ — memorise this one formula cold.

questions.q: The period of revolution of a charged particle in a cyclotron
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi m/(qB)$ has no $v$ or $r$ dependence, which is why a fixed-frequency oscillator can accelerate the particle throughout.
questions.trick: Cyclotron period $T=2\pi m/qB$ has no $v$ — always independent of speed.

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires carry currents of 3 A and 5 A in the same direction, separated by 2 cm. The force per unit length between them is
questions.explanation: $F/l = \mu_0I_1I_2/(2\pi d) = (4\pi\times10^{-7}\times3\times5)/(2\pi\times0.02) = (2\times10^{-7}\times15)/0.02 = 1.5\times10^{-4}$ N/m; currents in the same direction attract.
questions.trick: $F/l=\mu_0I_1I_2/2\pi d$; same direction currents ALWAYS attract.

questions.q: A straight wire of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T, perpendicular to the field. The force on the wire is
questions.explanation: $F = BIl = 0.2\times4\times0.5 = 0.4$ N.
questions.trick: $F=BIl$ — perpendicular case, no $\sin\theta$ factor needed.

questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 5 A, having 20 turns, is
questions.trick: $B=\mu_0NI/2R$ at coil centre — multiply by turns, don't forget.

questions.q: A long solenoid has 2000 turns per metre and carries a current of 5 A. The magnetic field inside it (away from the ends) is
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0nI = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2000\times5 = 4\pi\times10^{-3}$ T.
questions.trick: Solenoid: $B=\mu_0nI$, with $n$ = turns PER METRE, not total turns.

questions.q: A velocity selector uses perpendicular electric and magnetic fields of 4$\times10^4$ V/m and 0.2 T. The speed of the undeflected charged particle is
questions.explanation: Undeflected when $qE=qvB \Rightarrow v=E/B = 4\times10^4/0.2 = 2\times10^5$ m/s.
questions.trick: Velocity selector: undeflected speed is always $v=E/B$, simple ratio.

questions.q: A rectangular current loop of magnetic moment $m$ is placed with its plane parallel to a uniform magnetic field $B$. The torque on the loop is
questions.explanation: When the loop's plane is parallel to $B$, its normal (and $\vec m$) is perpendicular to $B$, so $\theta=90^\circ$: $\tau = mB\sin90^\circ = mB$, the maximum value.
questions.trick: Plane parallel to $B$ means $\vec m\perp\vec B$: torque is maximum, $\tau=mB$.

questions.q: A galvanometer with resistance 100 $\Omega$ and full-scale deflection current 1 mA is to be converted into an ammeter of range 1 A. The shunt resistance required is approximately
questions.explanation: $S = \dfrac{I_gG}{I-I_g} = \dfrac{10^{-3}\times100}{1-10^{-3}} \approx \dfrac{0.1}{1} = 0.1\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Shunt $S=I_gG/(I-I_g)$ — always much smaller than $G$ for ammeter conversion.

questions.q: To convert a galvanometer of resistance 50 $\Omega$ and full-scale current 2 mA into a voltmeter of range 10 V, the series resistance needed is
questions.trick: Series resistance $R=V/I_g-G$ — always much bigger than $G$ for voltmeter conversion.

questions.q: Ampere's circuital law states that $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}$ around a closed loop equals
options: $\mu_0$ times the total current in the circuit
questions.explanation: Ampere's law: $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0I_{enc}$, where $I_{enc}$ is only the current passing through the surface bounded by the loop.
questions.trick: Ampere's law uses only ENCLOSED current, ignore currents outside the loop.

questions.q: An electron moving parallel to a uniform magnetic field experiences a magnetic force of
questions.explanation: $F = qvB\sin\theta$; when velocity is parallel to $B$, $\theta=0$, so $F=0$.
questions.trick: Velocity parallel to $B$ → $\sin\theta=0$ → force is always zero.

questions.q: A toroid has mean radius 20 cm and 1000 turns, carrying a current of 2 A. The magnetic field inside the toroid is
questions.trick: Toroid: $B=\mu_0NI/2\pi r$ — same form as straight wire but with total turns $N$.

questions.q: The magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop, at a point far away such that $x \gg R$, falls off as
questions.explanation: $B = \mu_0NIR^2/[2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}]$; for $x\gg R$, this reduces to $B \propto R^2/x^3$, i.e. $1/x^3$, similar to a magnetic dipole field.
questions.trick: Far axial field of a loop falls as $1/x^3$ — dipole-like, remember the cube.

questions.q: In a moving coil galvanometer, the coil is wound on a light metallic (aluminium) frame mainly to provide
options: electromagnetic (eddy current) damping so the pointer settles quickly
questions.explanation: As the coil swings, eddy currents induced in the conducting (non-magnetic) frame oppose the motion, damping oscillations so the pointer comes to rest quickly without overshooting.
questions.trick: Aluminium frame in galvanometer = eddy-current damping, for quick, non-oscillating settling.

questions.q: A charged particle enters a magnetic field with velocity making an angle $\theta$ (not 0 or 90) with $\vec{B}$. Its path is
questions.explanation: The velocity component along $B$ is unaffected (uniform motion) while the perpendicular component causes circular motion; combined, the path is a helix.
questions.trick: Velocity at an angle (not 0/90) to $B$ → path is always a helix.

questions.q: Two identical circular coils, each carrying current $I$, are placed with the same centre and their planes perpendicular to each other. The resultant magnetic field at the centre is (each coil alone gives field $B_0$ there)
questions.explanation: The two fields are equal in magnitude ($B_0$) and mutually perpendicular, so the resultant is $\sqrt{B_0^2+B_0^2} = B_0\sqrt2$.
questions.trick: Perpendicular equal fields combine as $B_0\sqrt2$ (Pythagoras), same trick as force addition.

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is
questions.explanation: The SI unit of $B$ is the tesla (T), equal to Wb/m$^2$; gauss is a CGS unit ($1\,\text{T}=10^4$ G).
questions.trick: SI unit of $B$ is tesla; gauss is CGS ($1\,T=10^4\,G$) — don't confuse.

questions.q: A current loop placed in a uniform magnetic field behaves like a magnetic dipole. For the loop to be in stable equilibrium, its magnetic moment $\vec{m}$ must be
questions.explanation: Potential energy $U=-mB\cos\theta$ is minimum (stable) when $\theta=0$, i.e. $\vec m$ parallel to $\vec B$.
questions.trick: Stable equilibrium: $\vec m\parallel\vec B$ (minimum $U=-mB\cos\theta$), same logic as dipoles.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased by
options: decreasing the area of the coil
increasing the torsional constant of the spring
increasing the magnetic field and number of turns, and decreasing the torsional constant
questions.explanation: Current sensitivity $= NAB/k$; it increases with more turns $N$, larger area $A$, stronger field $B$, and a smaller torsional constant $k$.
questions.trick: Sensitivity $=NAB/k$: more turns/area/field, weaker spring, all raise sensitivity.

questions.q: The total force on a charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec v$ in the presence of both an electric field $\vec E$ and a magnetic field $\vec B$ is given by
questions.explanation: The Lorentz force combines the electric and magnetic contributions: $\vec F=q(\vec E+\vec v\times\vec B)$.
questions.trick: Lorentz force is the SUM of electric and magnetic parts: $q(\vec E+\vec v\times\vec B)$.

questions.q: According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field $dB$ due to a current element $Idl$ at a point, making angle $\theta$ with the line joining them, at distance $r$, is proportional to
questions.explanation: The Biot-Savart law gives $dB\propto\dfrac{Idl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, forming the basis for calculating fields due to current distributions.
questions.trick: Biot-Savart: $dB\propto Idl\sin\theta/r^2$ — same $\sin\theta$ pattern as force law.

questions.q: A proton (charge $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, mass $1.6\times10^{-27}$ kg) moves in a cyclotron in a magnetic field of 0.5 T. Its cyclotron frequency is approximately
questions.explanation: $f=\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.5}{2\pi\times1.6\times10^{-27}}\approx8\times10^6$ Hz.
questions.trick: Cyclotron frequency $f=qB/2\pi m$ — plug numbers directly, mass cancels the $2\pi$ shape.

questions.q: A proton and an electron, having the same speed, enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it. Since the proton is much more massive than the electron, the radius of its circular path is
options: the same as that of the electron
much smaller than that of the electron
much larger than that of the electron
questions.explanation: $r=mv/(qB)$; with the same $v$, $B$, and charge magnitude, $r\propto m$, so the much heavier proton follows a much larger radius.
questions.trick: $r\propto m$ (same $v,B,q$) — heavier particle always curves in a bigger circle.

questions.q: In a cyclotron, a charged particle gains kinetic energy $qV$ each time it crosses the gap between the dees, where $V$ is the accelerating voltage. Since it crosses the gap twice per revolution, the energy gained per revolution is
questions.explanation: The particle is accelerated once in each half of a revolution (twice per full revolution), gaining $qV$ each time, for a total of $2qV$ per revolution.
questions.trick: Two accelerations per revolution (once per dee gap): total energy gain $=2qV$.

questions.q: The cyclotron is not suitable for accelerating electrons to high energies mainly because
options: electrons cannot move in a magnetic field
the magnetic field cannot act on electrons
electrons quickly attain relativistic speeds, so their mass increases and they fall out of resonance with the fixed-frequency oscillator
questions.explanation: Because of their small mass, electrons quickly reach speeds where relativistic mass increase becomes significant, changing their cyclotron frequency and desynchronising them from the fixed oscillator frequency.
questions.trick: Electrons fail in cyclotrons: light mass → quickly relativistic → falls out of sync with fixed frequency.

questions.q: The voltage sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer, of coil resistance $R$, is defined as
options: deflection per unit voltage across the galvanometer, equal to $NAB/(kR)$
questions.explanation: Voltage sensitivity $=\theta/V=\dfrac{NAB}{kR}$, obtained by dividing the current sensitivity $NAB/k$ by the coil resistance $R$ (since $V=IR$).
questions.trick: Voltage sensitivity = current sensitivity$/R$: divide $NAB/k$ by coil resistance.

questions.q: In a moving coil galvanometer, the magnetic field is made radial (using concave pole pieces and a soft iron cylindrical core) so that
options: the plane of the coil is always parallel to the field, making the torque proportional to current at every deflection (linear scale)
questions.explanation: A radial field keeps the coil's plane always parallel to $B$ ($\theta=90^\circ$ throughout), so $\tau=NIAB$ stays proportional to $I$ at every deflection, giving a linear (uniform) scale.
questions.trick: Radial field keeps coil plane parallel to $B$ always → linear (uniform) scale.

questions.q: The magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are
options: concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire
straight lines parallel to the wire
questions.explanation: Around a long straight current-carrying wire, the magnetic field lines form concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it, with direction given by the right-hand thumb rule.
questions.trick: Straight wire's field: concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire, by right-hand rule.

questions.q: The magnetic field at a perpendicular distance of 5 cm from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is $B$. At a distance of 20 cm from the same wire, the field becomes
questions.explanation: $B=\mu_0I/(2\pi r)\propto1/r$; increasing $r$ by a factor of 4 (5 cm to 20 cm) reduces $B$ to $B/4$.
questions.trick: $B\propto1/r$ for a straight wire: distance $\times4$ means field $\to B/4$.

questions.q: A closed current loop of arbitrary shape is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net force on the loop is
options: zero, though it may experience a net torque
equal to $BIL$, where $L$ is the loop's perimeter
questions.explanation: In a uniform field, the forces on different current elements of a closed loop sum to zero net force, although a net torque can still act unless the loop's plane is perpendicular to the field.
questions.trick: Uniform field on a closed loop: net force is always zero, torque may still exist.

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle, having the same speed, enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to their velocity. Given that the alpha particle has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge of the proton, the ratio of the radius of the proton's circular path to that of the alpha particle's is
questions.explanation: $r=mv/(qB)$. $r_p=\dfrac{m v}{qB}$, $r_\alpha=\dfrac{4m\,v}{2qB}=\dfrac{2mv}{qB}=2r_p$. So $r_p:r_\alpha=1:2$.
questions.trick: $r\propto m/q$: compute the mass/charge ratio for each particle, then compare directly.

questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular current loop of radius $R$ is $B_0$. The field on the axis of the same loop, at a distance $x=R$ from the centre, is
questions.trick: At $x=R$ on axis, field drops to $B_0/2^{3/2}\approx0.354B_0$ — a value worth remembering.

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is
questions.explanation: Magnetic flux is measured in weber (Wb); tesla (Wb/m$^2$) is the unit of magnetic field.
questions.trick: Magnetic flux unit is weber; tesla is flux PER AREA — don't swap them.

questions.q: The magnetic field outside an ideal toroid, in the space surrounding it, is
questions.explanation: The winding confines the field entirely within the toroid's core; an Amperian loop drawn outside encloses zero net current, so $B=0$ outside an ideal toroid.
questions.trick: Ideal toroid: all field is confined inside the core — zero outside, always.

questions.q: One ampere is defined as the current which, when flowing through each of two long parallel wires kept 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force per unit length between them of
questions.explanation: Using $F/l=\mu_0I_1I_2/(2\pi d)$ with $I_1=I_2=1$ A and $d=1$ m gives $F/l=2\times10^{-7}$ N/m, which defines the ampere.
questions.trick: Ampere's definition: $2\times10^{-7}$ N/m per amp-pair at 1 m — the defining number.

questions.q: A current loop of magnetic moment $m$ is placed at an angle $\theta$ to a uniform field $B$. The magnitude of the torque on it is
questions.explanation: $\vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B$, so $\tau=mB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec m$ and $\vec B$.
questions.trick: Torque on a loop is always $mB\sin\theta$, never $\cos\theta$ or $\tan\theta$.

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires carry currents in opposite directions. The force between them is
questions.explanation: Currents in opposite directions in parallel wires repel each other; currents in the same direction attract.
questions.trick: Opposite-direction currents in parallel wires ALWAYS repel.

questions.q: A solenoid of length $l$ has $N$ turns and carries current $I$, producing a magnetic field $B$ inside it. If the number of turns is doubled (keeping the length and current the same), the new magnetic field is
questions.explanation: $B=\mu_0nI$ with $n=N/l$; doubling $N$ (at fixed $l$) doubles $n$ and hence $B$.
questions.trick: $B=\mu_0nI$, $n=N/l$: doubling turns (fixed length) directly doubles $B$.

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires, 20 cm apart, carry equal currents in the same direction. The magnetic field exactly midway between them (due to both wires) is
options: twice that due to one wire alone
equal to that due to one wire alone
questions.explanation: Between the wires, the fields due to the two equal, same-direction currents point in opposite directions (by the right-hand rule); being equidistant, they are equal in magnitude at the midpoint and exactly cancel.
questions.trick: Same-direction wires: fields between them point opposite ways and cancel at the midpoint.
